title: Handing back several values
summary: return a, b hands back a tuple, and the call unpacks it into names: low, high = min_max(xs). One name per value, or Python stops. A function can return early when there is nothing to do, and one with no return gives back None.
objectives: Return several values as a tuple.
Unpack the result into one name per value.
Return early for the empty or bad case.
Know that a function with no return gives None.

slides.h: By the end: a shelf summary in one call
slides.say: Meera wants three numbers about a shelf: how many books, the oldest year and the total copies. By the end one function will hand back all three, and one line will catch them.
points: `return a, b, c` returns a **tuple** of three values.
p: Meera wants three numbers about a shelf: how many books, the oldest year and the total copies. By the end one function will hand back all three, and one line will catch them.
`return a, b, c` returns a **tuple** of three values.

visual.text:
books = [
    {"title": "Wings of Fire", "author": "A. P. J. Abdul Kalam", "year": 1999, "copies": 3},
    {"title": "The Guide", "author": "R. K. Narayan", "year": 1958, "copies": 2},
    {"title": "Malgudi Days", "author": "R. K. Narayan", "year": 1943, "copies": 4},
    {"title": "Godan", "author": "Premchand", "year": 1936, "copies": 1},
]

def summary(books):
    years = [b["year"] for b in books]
    copies = sum(b["copies"] for b in books)
    return len(books), min(years), copies

count, oldest, copies = summary(books)
print(count, "books, oldest", oldest, ",", copies, "copies")

terms: values in a fixed order, written with commas: `(4, 1936, 10)`
putting each value of a tuple into its own name

slides.say: Unpacking needs exactly as many names as values. Too few or too many and Python stops with ValueError.
points: If you only need some, unpack them all and ignore the rest with `_`: `count, _, copies = summary(books)`.
p: Unpacking needs exactly as many names as values. Too few or too many and Python stops with ValueError.
If you only need some, unpack them all and ignore the rest with `_`: `count, _, copies = summary(books)`.

slides.say: Deal with the awkward case first and leave. The rest of the function can then assume things are fine.
points: `if not books: return None` before the real work.
A guard at the top beats an if around the whole body.
p: Deal with the awkward case first and leave. The rest of the function can then assume things are fine.
`if not books: return None` before the real work.

slides.say: A function that reaches its end without `return` gives back `None`. Printing inside a function is not handing a value back.
points: `x = show(books)` makes x None if show only prints.
p: A function that reaches its end without `return` gives back `None`. Printing inside a function is not handing a value back.
`x = show(books)` makes x None if show only prints.

tasks.prompt: It stops with ValueError. Fix the unpacking so it prints **20 days, fine ₹12, late: True**.
tasks.model:
def loan_info(days):
    fine = max(0, days - 14) * 2
    return days, fine, fine > 0

days, fine, late = loan_info(20)
print(f"{days} days, fine ₹{fine}, late: {late}")

bank.q: Why `return None` at the top for an empty list?
options: The rest of the function can then assume there is data (no dividing by 0)

points: `return a, b` hands back a tuple.
`x, y = f()`: one name per value; `_` for ones you don’t need.
Guard first: `if not items: return None`.
No return means None; print is not return.
